questions.question: How does PrairieFire achieve high update throughput in billion-scale SSD-based approximate nearest neighbor search without sacrificing search performance?
questions.answer: PrairieFire achieves high update throughput while maintaining excellent search performance through buffered updates, batched local rebuilds, cascaded adjustments, concurrency control, and CPU-GPU-SSD cooperation [2]. These co-designs avoid the frequent SSD accesses typically incurred by foreground insertions and the heavy background reassignments that repeatedly relocate each vector [2].

citations.text: The bottleneck lies in CPU-intensive update paths, where foreground insertions incur frequent SSD accesses and background reassignments repeatedly relocate each vector, making high update throughput difficult to achieve even by exhausting available hardware. In this paper, using buffered updates and batched local rebuilds, we develop PrairieFire with cascaded adjustments, concurrency control, and CPU-GPU-SSD cooperation. These co-designs avoid frequent SSD accesses in foreground updates and heavy background reassignments, achieving high update throughput while maintaining excellent search performance.

questions.question: How does AgentOnto utilize Iterative Ontology Preparation to refine enterprise knowledge representations for LLM agents?
questions.answer: AgentOnto utilizes Iterative Ontology Preparation to further improve the ontology through self-generated analysis tasks [1].

citations.snippet: Enterprise data analysis requires agents to connect analytical requests with knowledge distributed across databases, business documents, and existing example tasks. Without an explicit representation of this knowledge, an agent may produce incorrect...
citations.text: Enterprise data analysis requires agents to connect analytical requests with knowledge distributed across databases, business documents, and existing example tasks. Without an explicit representation of this knowledge, an agent may produce incorrect analytical results and cannot reliably incorporate feedback. We present AgentOnto, an ontology-guided LLM agent for enterprise data analytics. AgentOnto organizes heterogeneous enterprise knowledge into an ontology that directly guides analysis and incorporates confirmed feedback. Iterative Ontology Preparation further improves the ontology through self-generated analysis tasks. We evaluate AgentOnto on two public data sources. AgentOnto substantially outperforms representative methods, while module-level evaluations confirm the effectiveness of ontology construction, analysis, and updating. A real-world deployment further demonstrates its practical value in enterprise analytics

questions.question: What three techniques are introduced by the PUMA framework to accelerate large-scale string similarity joins using Jaro-Winkler distance?
questions.answer:
Based on the available sources, the approach for efficient Jaro-Winkler similarity joins is based on three key techniques (with the PUMA framework being part of them):

1. **JUMP**: A fast algorithm for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings that runs in linear time for bounded alphabets [1].
2. **Dual-bound intersection bitmaps**: Bitmaps that encode strings (represented as character sets) into fixed-size bitmaps, equipped with a cost model to adapt to input data and prune candidate string pairs by bounding character overlap [1].
3. **The PUMA framework**: Groups strings by prefix to tighten filter conditions, thereby reducing the number of similarity computations [1].

citations.snippet: We present a novel approach for efficient Jaro-Winkler similarity joins on large string collections. Our solution is based on three key techniques: (1) JUMP is a fast algorithm for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings that runs i...
citations.text: We present a novel approach for efficient Jaro-Winkler similarity joins on large string collections. Our solution is based on three key techniques: (1) JUMP is a fast algorithm for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings that runs in linear time for bounded alphabets. (2) Dual-bound intersection bitmaps encode strings -- represented as character sets -- into fixed-size bitmaps, which are used to prune candidate string pairs by providing effective bounds on their character overlap; unlike prior bitmap techniques, our bitmaps are equipped with a cost model and adapt to the input data. (3) Our PUMA framework groups strings by prefix to tighten filter conditions, thereby reducing the number of similarity computations. Extensive experiments on large string collections demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms the state of the art, achieving speedups of up to three orders of magnitude.

questions.question: What computational complexity is established for finding a diverse subset of why-provenance explanations in Datalog queries?
questions.answer: Based on the provided documents, the problem of finding a diverse subset of why-provenance explanations for Datalog queries is highly intractable, specifically being **NP-hard even in data complexity** [1].

citations.snippet: . However, whenever the set of explanations is very large, outputting the entire set might be prohibitively expensive. Moreover, it is questionable the practical usefulness of flooding the user with a very large number of explanations, many of them p...
citations.text: . However, whenever the set of explanations is very large, outputting the entire set might be prohibitively expensive. Moreover, it is questionable the practical usefulness of flooding the user with a very large number of explanations, many of them possibly differing only marginally. In this case, one can argue that it would be practically more useful to compute a small, sufficiently diverse subset of the set of why-provenance explanations. The present work initiates the study of the latter problem. In particular, we formalize the problem of interest as an optimization problem, and, after showing that it is highly intractable (it is NP-hard even in data complexity), we investigate whether ILP optimization solvers can be employed towards practical solutions. Our main finding is that this is achievable as long as we keep the requested set of explanations small, or we employ approximation algorithms (with error guarantees).

questions.question: How does the Helmholtz Component Flow Matching architecture isolate anomaly signals in time series without requiring full Jacobian-trace estimation?
questions.answer:
The Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM) framework isolates anomaly signals by parameterizing the vector field prediction network with three separate heads: a transport head, a compression head, and a residual head [1]. 

Specifically, it avoids expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field by applying the following structural constraints:
* **The transport head** is constrained to be divergence-free, ensuring that volume-preserving nominal transport is separated from density-changing behavior [1, 3].
* **The compression head** is exclusively restricted to handling divergence estimation, where local expansion and contraction (which carry anomaly-sensitive information) occur [1].
* **A lightweight residual head** is used to absorb any remaining mismatch [1, 3]. 

By separating these components, HCFM yields cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior without requiring expensive Jacobian-trace estimation across a monolithic vector field [1, 3].

citations.snippet: Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which...
citations.text: Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly-sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field. We propose \emph{Helmholtz Component Flow Matching} (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch

questions.question: How does the RemoteANN vector search engine minimize cloud object storage request fees and network I/O during similarity queries?
questions.answer:
To minimize cloud object storage request fees and network I/O during similarity queries, RemoteANN utilizes a co-designed data layout and query engine approach, which includes the following mechanisms [1]:

* **Tailored Data Layout:** It couples an Inverted File (IVF) index with RaBitQ quantization, and further optimizes this with inter-cluster and intra-cluster data reordering to improve data locality [1].
* **Query Engine Optimization:** Its query engine combines cluster pruning, fine-grained Range-GET requests, request merging, and local NVMe SSD caching [1]. 

Together, these techniques dramatically reduce discrete storage requests and network transfer volume without sacrificing accuracy [1].

citations.text: To resolve these challenges, we present RemoteANN, a vector search engine explicitly co-designed for cloud object storage across indexing and querying. To mitigate the dominant network I/O bottleneck, RemoteANN couples an Inverted File (IVF) index with RaBitQ quantization, further optimized by inter-cluster and intra-cluster data reordering for improved data locality. Building on this tailored data layout, RemoteANN's query engine combines cluster pruning, fine-grained Range-GET requests, request merging, and local NVMe SSD caching, dramatically reducing discrete storage requests and network transfer volume without sacrificing accuracy. To address the index construction bottleneck, we further develop QGKMeans, which substantially reduces construction latency without compromising clustering quality

questions.question: What diagnostic methodology does the MemDerive benchmark use to expose failures in agent memory systems over evolving histories?
questions.answer:
To expose failures in agent memory systems over evolving histories, the MemDerive benchmark uses the following diagnostic methodology:

* **Symbolic Scenario Specification:** It specifies each scenario symbolically and derives exact gold answers using Datalog [2].
* **Gold Derivation DAG and Supporting Events:** It records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events for every query [2].
* **Node Probing:** It diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG [3].
* **Reliability and Evolution Tracking:** It evaluates answer reliability and tracks whether answers remain correct as new events arrive [3].

citations.text: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition

citations.text: . Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.

questions.question: How does the SARP indexing scheme resolve the tradeoff between prefix-matching latency and crash-recovery time for on-SSD KVCache?
questions.answer:
SARP resolves the tradeoff between prefix-matching latency and crash-recovery time for on-SSD KVCache through the following mechanisms:

* **Avoiding Full Index Rebuilds:** Like other on-SSD indexes, SARP avoids the long recovery times associated with rebuilding a full snapshot-backed in-memory index after a crash or restart [1]. Instead, it quickly restores its sparse routing directory from a snapshot [2, 3].
* **Sparse In-Memory Routing and Segment Packing:** SARP uses a compact in-memory routing directory with entries at selected block positions to identify candidate segments, as extending a matched prefix over a short span usually distinguishes only a few token sequences [1, 2]. It groups consecutive block IDs and metadata into segments to amortize storage accesses across multiple blocks [2].
* **Optimized Retrieval and Filtering:** SARP limits segment retrievals and employs compact filters to prioritize candidates that have longer potential matches [2]. 
* **Sequential Metadata Access:** Because prefix matching accesses block metadata in sequence order, metadata for consecutive blocks can be retrieved together [1, 2]. After retrieval, SARP verifies the block IDs against the query to reuse KVCache blocks covered by the verified prefix [2, 3].

citations.text: Distributed LLM serving relies on a global index to locate reusable key-value cache (KVCache) blocks through prefix matching. Losing the index after a crash or restart forces affected requests to recompute existing KVCache on GPUs. Persisting the index restores access after a failure. Existing persistent indexes face a tension between prefix-matching performance and recovery time. A snapshot-backed in-memory index supports fast prefix matching, but rebuilding the full index delays recovery. An on-SSD index avoids this rebuild, but adds storage accesses to prefix matching. Our core insight is that extending a matched prefix over a short span typically requires distinguishing only a few token sequences, suggesting that sparse in-memory routing state may suffice. Prefix matching also accesses block metadata in sequence order, allowing metadata for consecutive blocks to be retrieved together

We present SARP (Sparse Adaptive Routing and Packing), an on-SSD KVCache index for fast recovery and prefix matching. SARP groups consecutive block IDs and metadata into segments to amortize storage accesses across multiple blocks. A compact in-memory routing directory identifies candidate segments using entries at selected block positions. SARP limits segment retrievals and uses compact filters to prioritize candidates with longer potential matches. questions.question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in the original Transformer architecture?
questions.answer:
In the original Transformer architecture, the multi-head self-attention layer plays several key roles:

* **Relating tokens and learning context:** It relates all relevant tokens to better encode every word, residue, or token in the input sequence, learning sequence-wide context information [1].
* **Capturing diverse relationships in parallel:** It performs attention through multiple parallel heads, allowing the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces, capture diverse relationships and patterns, and process information from multiple perspectives simultaneously [2, 3, 4, 5].
* **Generating contextualized representations:** Before calculating the attention function, each token embedding is transformed into corresponding Query ($Q$), Key ($K$), and Value ($V$) vectors to determine how strongly each token should attend to others [1, 2].

questions.question: How does Dijkstra's algorithm determine the shortest path from a single source vertex in a non-negative weighted graph?
questions.answer:
Based on the provided sources, Dijkstra's algorithm determines the shortest paths from a given source node to every other node in a weighted graph [1]. 

The step-by-step process operates as follows:
* **Initialization:** All vertices are assigned a tentative distance of infinity (`dist[v] ← INFINITY`), their previous node set to undefined (`prev[v] ← UNDEFINED`), and added to a set $Q$ of unvisited nodes [3]. The source node's distance is set to zero (`dist[source] ← 0`) [3].
* **Iteration:** While the set $Q$ is not empty, the algorithm selects the vertex $u$ in $Q$ that has the minimum distance `dist[u]` and removes it from $Q$ [3]. 
* **Edge Relaxation:** For each neighbor $v$ of $u$, it calculates an alternative distance (`alt ← dist[u] + Graph.Distance(u,v)`) [3]. If this alternative path is shorter than the currently recorded distance for $v$, `dist[v]` is updated to `alt`, and `prev[v]` is set to $u$ [3]. 
* **Completion:** After all nodes are visited, the shortest path from the source to any node consists only of visited nodes, making `dist[v]` the shortest distance [2]. The algorithm can also terminate early when finding the path to a specific destination node once that target node is selected with the minimum distance [1, 5].

citations.text:
Dijkstra's algorithm (, DYKE-strəz) is an algorithm for finding the shortest paths between nodes in a weighted graph, which may represent, for example, a road network. It was conceived by computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra in 1956 and published three years later.

Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a given source node to every other node. It can be used to find the shortest path to a specific destination node, by terminating the algorithm after determining the shortest path to that node. For example, if the nodes of the graph represent cities, and the costs of edges represent the distances between pairs of cities connected by a direct road, then Dijkstra's algorithm can be used to find the shortest route between one city and all other cities.

questions.question: How does a Bloom filter achieve space efficiency and why can it yield false positives but never false negatives?
questions.answer:
Based on the provided sources:

**How a Bloom filter achieves space efficiency:**
* It does not store the data items themselves (unlike data structures such as hash tables, trees, tries, or linked lists), requiring a separate solution for actual storage [3]. 
* It inherits compactness from arrays and utilizes a probabilistic nature [5]. 
* By using a generalized Bloom filter where $k$ (the number of hash functions) is greater than 1, about half of the bits are set when parameters are chosen well, which minimizes redundancy and maximizes information content [1].

**Why it can yield false positives but never false negatives:**
* A Bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure used to test set membership [2]. 
* False positives occur and increase as more items are added because multiple elements can map to the same bits in the array [2, 4]. 
* False negatives are not possible because if an element were in the set, all of its corresponding bits would definitely have been set when it was added [2].

citations.snippet: To understand its space efficiency, it is instructive to compare the general Bloom filter with its special case when k = 1.  If k = 1, then in order to keep the false positive rate sufficiently low, a small fraction of bits should be set, which means...
citations.text: To understand its space efficiency, it is instructive to compare the general Bloom filter with its special case when k = 1.  If k = 1, then in order to keep the false positive rate sufficiently low, a small fraction of bits should be set, which means the array must be very large and contain long runs of zeros.  The information content of the array relative to its size is low.  The generalized Bloom filter (k greater than 1) allows many more bits to be set while still maintaining a low false positive rate; if the parameters (k and m) are chosen well, about half of the bits will be set, and these will be apparently random, minimizing redundancy and maximizing information content.

citations.snippet: In computing, a Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure, conceived by Burton Howard Bloom in 1970, that is used to test whether an element is a member of a set. False positive matches are possible, but false negatives are not –...
citations.text: In computing, a Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure, conceived by Burton Howard Bloom in 1970, that is used to test whether an element is a member of a set. False positive matches are possible, but false negatives are not – in other words, a query returns either "possibly in set" or "definitely not in set". Elements can be added to the set, but not removed (though this can be addressed with the counting Bloom filter variant); the more items added, the larger the probability of false positives.

citations.snippet: While risking false positives, Bloom filters have a substantial space advantage over other data structures for representing sets, such as self-balancing binary search trees, tries, hash tables, or simple arrays or linked lists of the entries. Most of...
citations.text: While risking false positives, Bloom filters have a substantial space advantage over other data structures for representing sets, such as self-balancing binary search trees, tries, hash tables, or simple arrays or linked lists of the entries. Most of these require storing at least the data items themselves, which can require anywhere from a small number of bits, for small integers, to an arbitrary number of bits, such as for strings (tries are an exception since they can share storage between elements with equal prefixes).  However, Bloom filters do not store the data items at all, and a separate solution must be provided for the actual storage. Linked structures incur an additional linear space overhead for pointers.

citations.snippet: A Bloom filter with a 1% error and an optimal value of k, in contrast, requires only about 9.6 bits per element, regardless of the size of the elements. This advantage comes partly from its compactness, inherited from arrays, and partly from its prob...
citations.text:
A Bloom filter with a 1% error and an optimal value of k, in contrast, requires only about 9.6 bits per element, regardless of the size of the elements. This advantage comes partly from its compactness, inherited from arrays, and partly from its probabilistic nature. The 1% false-positive rate can be reduced by a factor of ten by adding only about 4.8 bits per element.

However, if the number of potential values is small and many of them can be in the set, the Bloom filter is easily surpassed by the deterministic bit array, which requires only one bit for each potential element. Hash tables gain a space and time advantage if they begin ignoring collisions and store only whether each bucket contains an entry; in this case, they have effectively become Bloom filters with k = 1.

questions.question: How does TCP congestion control use slow start and additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) to prevent network congestion?
questions.answer:
Based on the provided sources, TCP congestion control uses a multi-faceted strategy combining slow start, an additive increase/multiplicative decrease (AIMD) scheme, and a congestion window (CWND) to avoid congestive collapse and prevent network congestion [1, 2]:

* **Slow Start:** TCP begins with a small congestion window size (1, 2, 4, or 10 MSS) [3, 4]. During slow start, the transmission rate and window size are increased by 1 MSS with each received acknowledgment (ACK)—effectively doubling the window size each round-trip time (RTT)—until a packet loss is detected, the receiver's advertised window becomes the limiting factor, or the slow start threshold (ssthresh) is reached [3, 5]. 
* **Additive Increase / Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD):** Once the slow start threshold is reached, TCP switches to the congestion avoidance algorithm [5]. Under the AIMD approach, if all segments are received and acknowledgments arrive on time, the congestion window is linearly increased (e.g., by adding a constant or using formulas like increasing CWND by MSS * MSS / CWND for each RTT) [4, 5]. When congestion occurs, the algorithm applies an exponential reduction to the window size [2]. Multiple flows using AIMD will eventually converge to use equal shares of a contended link [2].

citations.snippet: To avoid congestive collapse, TCP uses a multi-faceted congestion-control strategy. For each connection, TCP maintains a CWND, limiting the total number of unacknowledged packets that may be in transit end-to-end. This is somewhat analogous to TCP's...
citations.text:
To avoid congestive collapse, TCP uses a multi-faceted congestion-control strategy. For each connection, TCP maintains a CWND, limiting the total number of unacknowledged packets that may be in transit end-to-end. This is somewhat analogous to TCP's sliding window used for flow control.

The additive increase/multiplicative decrease (AIMD) algorithm is a closed-loop control algorithm. AIMD combines linear growth of the congestion window with an exponential reduction when congestion occurs. Multiple flows using AIMD congestion control will eventually converge to use equal amounts of a contended link.

This is the algorithm that is described in RFC 5681 for the congestion avoidance state.

citations.snippet: The transmission rate will be increased by the slow-start algorithm until either a packet loss is detected, the receiver's advertised window (rwnd) becomes the limiting factor, or slow start threshold (ssthresh) is reached, which is used to determine...
citations.text:
The transmission rate will be increased by the slow-start algorithm until either a packet loss is detected, the receiver's advertised window (rwnd) becomes the limiting factor, or slow start threshold (ssthresh) is reached, which is used to determine whether the slow start or congestion avoidance algorithm is used, a value set to limit slow start.

If the CWND reaches ssthresh, TCP switches to the congestion avoidance algorithm. It should be increased by up to 1 MSS for each RTT. A common formula is that each new ACK increases the CWND by MSS * MSS / CWND. It increases almost linearly and provides an acceptable approximation.

questions.question: What distinct purpose do convolutional layers and pooling layers serve in a convolutional neural network?
questions.answer:
Based on the provided sources, the distinct purposes are:

* **Convolutional layers** apply a convolution operation to the input (by sliding a kernel or filter across it and computing a dot product) to extract features and generate feature maps [1], [3], [5].
* **Pooling layers** systematically reduce the spatial dimensions (width and height) of the feature maps by combining the outputs of neuron clusters into a single neuron, which decreases computation, makes the network less sensitive to the precise location of features, and introduces a degree of translation invariance [2], [5].

citations.snippet: A convolutional neural network consists of an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer. In a convolutional neural network, the hidden layers include one or more layers that perform convolutions. Typically this includes a layer that performs a d...
citations.text:
A convolutional neural network consists of an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer. In a convolutional neural network, the hidden layers include one or more layers that perform convolutions. Typically this includes a layer that performs a dot product of the convolution kernel with the layer's input matrix. This product is usually the Frobenius inner product, and its activation function is commonly ReLU. As the convolution kernel slides along the input matrix for the layer, the convolution operation generates a feature map, which in turn contributes to the input of the next layer. This is followed by other layers such as pooling layers, fully connected layers, and normalization layers.

Here it should be noted how close a convolutional neural network is to a matched filter.

citations.snippet: Convolutional networks may include local and/or global pooling layers along with traditional convolutional layers. Pooling layers reduce the dimensions of data by combining the outputs of neuron clusters at one layer into a single neuron in the next...
citations.text: Convolutional networks may include local and/or global pooling layers along with traditional convolutional layers. Pooling layers reduce the dimensions of data by combining the outputs of neuron clusters at one layer into a single neuron in the next layer. Local pooling combines small clusters, tiling sizes such as 2 × 2 are commonly used. Global pooling acts on all the neurons of the feature map. There are two common types of pooling in popular use: max and average. Max pooling uses the maximum value of each local cluster of neurons in the feature map, while average pooling takes the average value.

citations.snippet: In artificial neural networks, a convolutional layer is a type of network layer that applies a convolution operation to the input. Convolutional layers are some of the primary building blocks of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a class of neural...
citations.text:
In artificial neural networks, a convolutional layer is a type of network layer that applies a convolution operation to the input. Convolutional layers are some of the primary building blocks of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a class of neural network most commonly applied to images, video, audio, and other data that have the property of uniform translational symmetry.

The convolution operation in a convolutional layer involves sliding a small window (called a kernel or filter) across the input data and computing the dot product between the values in the kernel and the input at each position. This process creates a feature map that represents detected features in the input.

citations.snippet: Convolution layers extract features from input data, generating feature maps. These maps, while informative, often retain a high spatial resolution (width and height). Processing these large maps in subsequent layers can be computationally expensive...
citations.text:
Convolution layers extract features from input data, generating feature maps. These maps, while informative, often retain a high spatial resolution (width and height). Processing these large maps in subsequent layers can be computationally expensive and may make the network overly sensitive to the precise location of features within the input. Pooling layers offer a way to address this by systematically reducing the spatial dimensions of the feature maps. [...] Pooling layers are typically inserted between successive convolutional layers (usually after the activation function applied to the convolution output). A common pattern in CNNs is:

CONV -> ReLU -> POOL -> CONV -> ReLU -> POOL -> ... -> Flatten -> Fully Connected -> Output [...] In summary, pooling is a fundamental operation in CNNs that reduces the spatial dimensions of feature maps, decreases computation, and introduces a degree of translation invariance, complementing the feature extraction role of convolutional layers. Max pooling is the most frequently used variant due to its effectiveness in preserving strong feature activations.

questions.question: What properties define a B-tree and keep it balanced during insertions and deletions?
questions.answer:
A B-tree is defined by the following properties:
* It is a self-balancing tree data structure that maintains sorted data and generalizes the binary search tree by allowing nodes to have more than two children (referred to as an $m$-way tree, where $m$ represents the maximum number of children a node can have) [1], [2].
* It stores multiple keys per node and ensures that interior nodes are at least half full [3], [4].

To keep the tree balanced during insertions and deletions:
* **Insertions:** When a new key is inserted and a node exceeds its maximum capacity, the node is split into two siblings, and the mid-value key is pushed up into the parent [3], [4]. The depth of the tree only increases when the root is split [4].
* **Deletions:** When a key is removed and a node falls below the minimum capacity, the tree is rebalanced by either redistributing keys from sibling nodes or merging nodes together [3], [4].

In computer science, a B-tree is a self-balancing tree data structure that maintains sorted data and allows searches, sequential access, insertions, and deletions in logarithmic time. The B-tree generalizes the binary search tree, allowing nodes to have more than two children.

By allowing more children under one node than a regular self-balancing binary search tree, the B-tree reduces the height of the tree and puts the data in fewer separate blocks. This is especially important for trees stored in secondary storage (e.g., disk drives), as these systems have relatively high latency and work with relatively large blocks of data, hence the B-tree's use in databases and file systems.

# B-Trees: Efficient Database Indexing Structures

B-Trees are self-balancing tree data structures that maintain sorted data and allow searches, sequential access, insertions, and deletions in logarithmic time. They are optimized for systems that read and write large blocks of data and are commonly used in databases and file systems.

B-Tree Operations Animation

## Key Properties of B-Trees [...] Reduced Disk I/O: By storing multiple keys per node, B-Trees minimize the number of disk accesses required for operations.
 Optimized for External Storage: The structure is designed specifically for block-based storage systems like hard drives and SSDs.
 Consistent Performance: Due to the balanced nature of B-Trees, worst-case performance remains logarithmic regardless of insertion or deletion patterns. [...] ## B-Tree Operations

The three main operations in a B-Tree are:

1. Search: Begin at the root and recursively traverse down the tree based on key comparisons until finding the target key or reaching a leaf node.
2. Insert: Find the appropriate leaf node for the new key, insert it, and if the node exceeds maximum capacity, split it and propagate changes upward.
3. Delete: Remove the key, and if the node falls below minimum capacity, either redistribute keys from siblings or merge nodes.

questions.question: What are the latest experimental breakthroughs in quantum computing qubit coherence times announced this week?
questions.answer:
Based on the provided sources, recent breakthroughs in qubit coherence times include:

* **Princeton University:** A research team at Princeton achieved a superconducting qubit that retains its quantum state for over 1 millisecond (coherence times longer than 1 ms), which is roughly three times longer than previous records and nearly 15 times longer than the industry standard [2, 4]. This was achieved by making material changes to the qubits—specifically changing the superconductor from aluminum to tantalum and the substrate from sapphire to silicon [5]—marking the largest single improvement and advance in qubit lifetime/coherence time in over a decade [2, 4]. 
* **University of Chicago:** A research team from the Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (led by David Awshalom and his team) identified a simple method—adding an exquisitely tailored oscillating magnetic field—to maintain qubit coherence 10,000 times longer than before (up to four orders of magnitude) [1].

questions.question: What are the latest developments and legal enforcement timelines for AI regulation in the European Union and the United States this week?
questions.answer:
Based on the available sources, here are the legal enforcement timelines and developments for the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act):

* **12 July 2024:** The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) was published in the EU Official Journal [1].
* **1 August 2024:** The EU AI Act officially entered into force across all 27 EU Member States (20 days after its publication) [1].
* **2 February 2025:** The first major enforcement deadline occurred, bringing the AI-system definition, prohibited-practice framework, and bans on prohibited uses into application [2, 3, 5].
* **2 August 2025:** Enforcement of certain requirements began, including notification obligations, governance, rules on General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models, confidentiality, and penalties (excluding penalties for providers of GPAI models) [1, 5]. *(Providers of GPAI models placed on the EU market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to comply [1]).*
* **2 August 2026:** The enforcement of the majority of the Act's provisions—including requirements for high-risk systems—commences [1, 5].
* **2 December 2026:** Prohibitions on AI systems generating non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material (CSAM) become applicable [4].
* **2 August 2030:** AI components of Union large-scale IT systems in the area of freedom, security, and justice placed on the market before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance [2].

The provided context does not contain sufficient information to answer regarding developments or legal enforcement timelines for the United States.

16 min read

Google Cloud’s revenue jumped 82% year-over-year to $24.8 billion in the quarter ended June 2026, accelerating from 63% growth on $20.0 billion in revenue the quarter before, and beating Wall Street’s already-aggressive forecast of roughly 64% growth. Alphabet reported the number on July 22. One week later, on July 30, Amazon reports its own second-quarter results, and the gap between these growth rates has become the central story of this earnings season. [...] Alphabet’s second-quarter 2026 results, released July 22, showed Google Cloud revenue of $24.8 billion, up 82% year-over-year — a figure CRN’s coverage of Synergy Research Group’s market-share data also confirmed — and accelerating from the prior quarter’s 63% growth rate. Analysts had penciled in roughly 64% growth, making the print a clear beat. It also topped Google Cloud’s own first-quarter growth rate of 63%, a figure Axis Intelligence linked to Google Cloud’s 14% share of the global cloud [...] The trend holds across every row. Google Cloud grew faster, converted more of that growth into profit, and kept signing bigger multi-year contracts in the June quarter than in the March quarter. The backlog is the figure worth watching most closely: it jumped to $514 billion, up from just $106 billion a year earlier, and just over half of it is expected to convert into recognized revenue within the next 24 months.

Google Cloud is expected to again lead the three major players in ​the September quarter, with revenue surging 95.1% to $29.57 billion, according to LSEG data. That would be faster than the 81.8% growth in the previous quarter. [...] Analysts expect Azure to post sales of $33.06 billion in the quarter, powering a 16.7% rise in Microsoft's total revenue to $90.66 billion, slightly slower growth ​than the previous period.

Amazon's overall revenue growth is expected to slow to 12.3% from 19.6% in the previous quarter.
